claims.text: The starting material is an equiatomic CoCrFeNiTi powder mixture.
The initial powder has coarse grains and high porosity.
Ti content and low lattice strain give equiatomic CoCrFeNiTi a thermodynamic tendency to form an HCP phase.
Six hours of high-energy ball milling generates enough lattice strain and grain refinement to lower the energy barrier for a metastable FCC-to-BCC solid-solution transition.
SPS at 1000°C facilitates densification of the milled CoCrFeNiTi powder.
SPS at 1000°C stabilizes a refined FCC/BCC dual-phase structure without excessive Ti-driven HCP precipitation.
The equiatomic CoCrFeNiTi composition has or can maintain a VEC near 8.0, identified as an FCC stability threshold.
VEC and atomic-radius mismatch govern the proposed FCC/BCC phase stability and can be controlled to prevent HCP nucleation.
Six-hour milling produces a high density of dislocations and sub-100 nm grains.
Milling-generated dislocations and nanocrystalline grain boundaries act as nucleation sites for the metastable FCC/BCC solid solution.
The milling-generated defects inhibit diffusion-controlled growth of Ti-rich HCP phases during SPS.
The rapid SPS thermal cycle preserves grain-boundary strengthening while enabling densification.
The 1000°C SPS cycle does not provide enough thermal energy for Ti segregation into HCP Laves phases.
The resulting CoCrFeNiTi alloy will be fully dense with negligible porosity.
The resulting alloy will have an FCC/BCC dual-phase microstructure.
The alloy will exceed 400 HV and be harder than cast counterparts because of grain-boundary and solid-solution strengthening.
Excessive HCP precipitation causes brittleness in CoCrFeNiTi.
Conventionally cast or briefly milled CoCrFeNiTi typically has coarse grains, residual porosity, dominant HCP phase, low hardness, and brittleness.
Sintering above 1050°C causes excessive grain growth that defeats kinetic stabilization.
Milling beyond eight hours causes thermodynamic decomposition into brittle Ti-driven HCP phases.

contradictions.description: An equiatomic CoCrFeNiTi composition has a nominal VEC of about 7.4 using the conventional Co=9, Cr=6, Fe=8, Ni=10, and Ti=4 values, not the stated value near 8.0. No compositional adjustment is proposed that could maintain VEC near 8.0.

The boundary assigns temperatures above 1050°C to excessive grain growth and milling beyond eight hours to HCP decomposition, respectively, but the falsification rule treats increased HCP fraction at 1100°C as the predicted temperature-boundary response.

The hypothesis requires VEC and radius mismatch to remain within an FCC stability window while simultaneously predicting a substantial FCC-to-BCC transition and stable FCC/BCC dual phase; the relationship between the claimed FCC window and BCC stabilization is not resolved.
